questions.q: You test 20 metrics, each at alpha = 0.05, and every null hypothesis is actually true. Roughly what is the chance at least one comes out significant?
options: About 5%
About 64%
About 20%
Exactly 0%, since the nulls are true
questions.explain: 1 - 0.95^20 is about 0.64. Each test has a 5% false-alarm chance, and the chances accumulate across tests.

questions.q: What does the Bonferroni correction do with 20 tests and alpha = 0.05?
options: Multiplies every p-value by 0.05
Discards the 5% smallest p-values
Tests each hypothesis at 0.05 / 20 = 0.0025
Runs the tests again on new data
questions.explain: Bonferroni divides alpha by the number of tests to control the family-wise error rate. It is simple but conservative.

questions.q: How do FWER and FDR differ?
options: They are two names for the same thing
FWER is the chance of at least one false discovery; FDR is the expected proportion of discoveries that are false
FWER applies only to t-tests and FDR only to chi-square tests
FDR controls Type II errors and FWER controls Type I errors
questions.explain: FWER guards against any false discovery; FDR tolerates some false discoveries as long as they are a small share of all discoveries, which retains more power.

questions.q: In the lesson's simulated run with 6 real effects among 20 metrics, Bonferroni flagged 5 and Benjamini-Hochberg flagged 6, neither with false alarms. What does this illustrate?
options: Benjamini-Hochberg is always better
Stricter error control tends to cost power, so a conservative correction can miss real effects
Corrections never change which results are significant
Bonferroni is wrong
questions.explain: Bonferroni's stricter control missed one real effect. It's one illustrative run, not proof that any method is universally better; the right choice depends on the cost of false discoveries versus misses.

questions.q: Which practice best reduces the multiple comparisons problem before you even analyze the data?
options: Running as many segment cuts as possible and reporting the significant ones
Changing alpha after seeing the results
Declaring one primary metric in advance and treating everything else as exploratory
Only reporting p-values, never effect sizes
questions.explain: A single pre-declared primary metric needs no correction, and exploratory findings can be confirmed in fresh data.
